(1) 
In the Supreme Court of the United States
───────────
No. 26A476
FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION, APPLICANT
v. 
SHERROD BROWN, ET AL. 
───────────
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF APPLICATION FOR STAY
───────────
The challengers fail to rehabilitate the Fourth Circuit’s order directing the 
Commission to act within 48 hours on their application for review of the Media Bureau’s public notice, which restated a longstanding position adopted during previous 
election cycles. First, this Court’s prior stay order held that FCC review is an essential predicate to judicial review under the Communications Act. Yet the challengers 
would reduce the FCC’s role to a meaningless ritual, arguing (Opp. 20) that the FCC
should issue an order that says, “Denied,” so that the Fourth Circuit can get on with 
telling everyone what the statutory lowest-unit-charge requirement really means. 
Second, mandamus is available only where it is clear and indisputable that an agency 
has unreasonably delayed taking action. But the challengers do not identify a single 
case in which any other court has ever held that a period as short as here triggers
that demanding standard. Third, mandamus must be appropriate in the circumstances of the case. The challengers fail to justify judicial intervention to overturn a 
longstanding agency position just weeks before this year’s elections, when parties and 
candidates need certainty about advertising rates. This Court should reject the challengers’ invitation to cause electoral chaos and should grant the application for a stay.

2 
A. This Court Is Likely To Reverse The Grant Of Mandamus
1. At the outset, the challengers fail to reconcile the Fourth Circuit’s grant 
of mandamus with this Court’s prior stay order. See NRCC v. Brown, No. 26A274, 
slip op. (Sept. 4, 2026). In that order, the Court explained that the Communications 
Act “contemplates that an aggrieved party will file an application for review with the 
Commission, that the Commission will resolve that application by order, and that 
public notice of that order will issue before an aggrieved party may petition for further review in federal court.” Id. at 3. The scheme established by the statute, and 
enforced by this Court’s order, reflects Congress’s judgment that “full agency deliberations have something worthwhile to contribute” before judicial review begins. 2026 
WL 2493115, at *22 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). In granting mandamus, however, the 
Fourth Circuit treated FCC action as a mere box-checking exercise, directing the 
agency to issue a decision within 48 hours even though the comment period on an 
overlapping application for review remains open. The challengers similarly treat
FCC action as an empty formality, insisting (Opp. 20), as the panel did below, that 
the Commission “was not required to provide any reasoning.” See Appl. App. 16a 
(“[T]he Commission is not legally obligated to explain or justify its decision.”). This 
Court surely did not issue its prior stay just to invite the Fourth Circuit to compel the 
FCC to perform that hollow ceremony in order to facilitate the immediate re-issuance 
of the Fourth Circuit’s merits ruling. 
In addition, this Court’s prior stay order reflected the equitable judgment that 
the lowest-unit-charge rules should remain stable “in the critical weeks leading up to 
the midterms.” NRCC, slip op. 3. That is presumably why the Court issued its order 
on September 4, the date that the lowest-unit-charge requirement took effect for this 
election cycle. See Appl. App. 28a (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The Fourth Circuit

3 
“ignored [this] Court’s concern and unraveled its work” through a last-minute “intrusion into the nation’s electoral process.” Id. at 25a. 
2. Even putting aside this Court’s prior stay order, the government is likely 
to prevail because the challengers have not shown a clear and indisputable right to 
relief. The challengers fail to identify any case in which any court has ever held that 
an agency’s allowing an application for review without a statutory deadline to remain 
pending for a few months amounts to “unreasonabl[e] delay,” 5 U.S.C. 706(1), warranting mandamus relief. To the contrary, they concede (Opp. 17), with considerable
understatement, that “delays of this length may not typically trigger mandamus relief.” That alone provides an adequate basis for a stay. 
The challengers claim (Opp. 17) that the “unique circumstances of this case” 
justify mandamus, but just the opposite is true. To start, the challengers themselves 
have contributed to the delay by filing a baseless petition for review, seemingly triggering the court of appeals’ “exclusive jurisdiction,” 28 U.S.C. 2349(a), and raising 
doubts about whether the FCC even had the authority to act while the petition for 
review remained pending. Even apart from those doubts, it was hardly unreasonable 
for the FCC to refrain from acting while parallel litigation was proceeding in court. 
It made little sense for the Commission to devote time and energy to an application 
for review that, according to the challengers, it had already “constructively denied.” 
In addition, the comment period for the challengers’ application for review 
closed on September 30, and the comment period for the broadcasters’ overlapping 
application remains open. See Stay Appl. 5-6. An agency does not engage in unreasonable delay by waiting to receive and consider relevant comments—especially 
where, as here, it has shortened its usual comment period to accommodate the challengers’ desire for expedition. See id. at 11. The challengers now suggest (Opp. 18)

4 
that the solicitation of public comments is a ruse designed to delay judicial review. 
But it was entirely appropriate for the FCC to solicit public comments, given that the
Fourth Circuit, the challengers, and television broadcasters all previously criticized 
it for failing to take that very step. See Appl. App. 7a (Fourth Circuit faulting the 
FCC for failing “to solicit public comment”); Stay Opp. at 25, NRCC, supra (No. 
26A274) (challengers objecting that the FCC “did not seek public comment”); id.
Supp. App. at 21 (broadcasters objecting to the lack of “notice or public comment”). 
If that were not enough, it is also reasonable for the FCC to defer action on the 
challengers’ application for review until after this year’s elections. As noted, the Media Bureau’s public notice reaffirmed a longstanding interpretation that the Bureau 
had applied across previous election cycles. This Court has repeatedly emphasized 
that courts should refrain from changing election rules in the period immediately 
before an election. See, e.g., Purcell v. Gonzalez, 549 U.S. 1, 7-8 (2006) (per curiam). 
The FCC is entitled to conclude that it should likewise refrain from acting on the 
application for review during the election campaign, lest it create confusion about the 
meaning of the lowest-unit-charge requirement after the requirement has already 
taken effect. 
The challengers’ contrary arguments lack merit. The challengers observe 
(Opp. 16-17) that no agency rule sets a specific deadline for the Commission to act on 
their application. But that just means that the Commission is entitled to decide, on 
a case-by-case basis, how much time to take. A court is entitled to intervene only if 
it is clear and indisputable that the Commission has engaged in unreasonable delay, 
and the challengers have fallen well short of that standard here. 
The challengers also argue (Opp. 18) that, because the FCC’s briefs contain a 
“forceful defense” of the Media Bureau’s public notice, the FCC Commissioners do not

5 
“need [more] time to make up their minds and prepare a reasoned decision.” But 
what the FCC’s General Counsel says in a brief does not necessarily reflect what the 
FCC’s Commissioners will ultimately decide in an order. After all, it is a foundational
principle of administrative law that statements made by agency lawyers in litigation 
are not equivalent to decisions made by the agency itself. See, e.g., Burlington Truck 
Lines, Inc. v. United States, 371 U.S. 156, 168-169 (1962) (“The court may not accept 
counsel’s post hoc rationalizations for agency action[.] * * * For the courts to substitute * * * counsel’s discretion for that of the Commission is incompatible with the 
orderly functioning of the process of judicial review.”). In all events, even if the FCC 
Commissioners had made up their minds, it would be reasonable for them to release 
their decision after, rather than during, the ongoing election campaign. 
The challengers likewise suggest (Opp. 18) that, because this case involves a 
“pure question of statutory interpretation” that courts must decide de novo, further 
FCC deliberations are pointless. But the Communications Act’s requirement that 
FCC review precede judicial review contains no exception for questions of statutory 
interpretation. See 47 U.S.C. 155(c). That is presumably because Congress deemed 
FCC review valuable even for such questions. Moreover, although agencies’ views on 
statutory questions are not entitled to deference, they are entitled to “respectful consideration.” Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369, 386 (2024). It is 
inconsistent with the respect that courts owe to agencies, and with the role that the 
Communications Act’s review scheme envisions for the FCC, to demand that the FCC 
“simply * * * issu[e] an order that sa[ys], ‘Denied,’” Opp. 20, so that the Fourth Circuit can get on with deciding for itself what the statute really means. 
In the end, the challengers’ theory boils down to the notion that, because the 
Media Bureau’s public notice concerns campaign finance, the FCC was required to

6 
act on their application fast enough to enable judicial review before this year’s midterm elections. That premise is flawed. It is commonplace for contested campaignfinance rules to remain in effect for one or more election cycles before courts eventually resolve disputes about their lawfulness. See, e.g., NRSC v. FEC, 146 S. Ct. 2404, 
2414 (2026) (resolving in 2026 campaign-finance case that began during the 2022 
election cycle). Nothing in the Communications Act requires otherwise. The statute 
entitles the challengers to an FCC decision on their application, see 47 U.S.C. 
155(c)(4), but it does not guarantee them a decision on the expedited timeline they 
prefer—particularly where, as here, the challenged policy has been in place for years 
before this election cycle. Indeed, mandamus is especially unwarranted given that 
the parties most directly affected by the Bureau’s notice—the broadcasters forced to 
charge lower rates for certain political advertising—are not demanding pre-election 
judicial review, and that the challengers’ purported indirect harm consists of nothing 
more than a desire for political speech to cost more money for both the candidates 
they oppose and those they themselves support. 
3. The government is independently likely to succeed because mandamus
is plainly inappropriate given the challengers’ unreasonable delay in seeking relief. 
The Media Bureau’s public notice was issued on March 30, and the challengers waited 
a whole month before seeking FCC review on April 29. See Stay Appl. 4. They then 
wasted several more months in pursuing the baseless jurisdictional theory that the 
Fourth Circuit could intervene even before the FCC acted—a theory that would have
enabled them to evade the heightened standard for mandamus. See id at 4-5. Only 
in September, after that tactic failed and more than five months after the Media Bureau issued its public notice, did they finally seek mandamus. See id. at 5. The 
challengers cannot excuse that delay by claiming (Opp. 22) that, if they “had sought

7 
mandamus relief sooner,” the FCC would have argued that “too little time had 
passed.” In the FCC’s view, mandamus would not be appropriate at any time before 
this year’s elections. But if mandamus were appropriate at all, it should have been 
sought back in June, when the challengers petitioned for judicial review—not now, 
weeks before the midterms, after the lowest-unit charge requirement has taken effect
and been in force since September 4. 
To grant mandamus at this late date would be inconsistent with the equitable 
principle that courts generally should not tinker with election rules shortly before an 
election. See Purcell, 549 U.S. at 7-8. Overturning the Media Bureau’s interpretation 
of the lowest-unit-charge requirement now, after the requirement has already taken 
effect for this year’s elections, would “lead to disruption and to unanticipated and 
unfair consequences for candidates [and] political parties.” Merrill v. Milligan, 142 
S. Ct. 879, 881 (2022) (Kavanaugh, J., concurring). The challengers have no response
to that point, beyond repeating their erroneous arguments (Opp. 22-23) that any delay is attributable to the FCC rather than to their own flawed litigation choices. 
B. The Other Factors Favor A Stay
Contrary to the challengers’ suggestion (Opp. 12-13), this case warrants this 
Court’s review. The Fourth Circuit countermanded the stay order that this Court 
previously issued, violated the principle that courts should not toy with election rules 
in the period preceding an election, and disregarded well-established limits on the 
scope of mandamus. The challengers observe (Opp. 13) that they have not found “any 
case where this Court has granted certiorari to review a lower court’s equitable finding that an agency had unlawfully delayed taking a discrete action,” but that is only 
because the Fourth Circuit’s egregious decision is unprecedented—as confirmed by 
the challengers’ failure to cite a single case granting mandamus to compel agency

8 
action after a period of delay as short as the one at issue here. This Court’s intervention is thus warranted because the Fourth Circuit “use[d] a writ of mandamus more 
aggressively * * * than has ever yet been attempted.” Appl. App. 27a (Wilkinson, J., 
dissenting); see Sup. Ct. R. 10(a) and (c) (certiorari appropriate when a court of appeals resolves a federal question “in a way that conflicts with relevant decisions of 
this Court” or “depart[s] from the accepted and usual course of judicial proceedings”). 
The challengers are also wrong to deny (Opp. 25) that the Fourth Circuit’s order causes irreparable harm to the FCC. An agency plainly suffers irreparable harm 
when a court “demands at gunpoint an agency decision” within 48 hours. Appl. App. 
28a (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The challengers observe (Opp. 25) that the FCC has 
a statutory obligation to act on their application for review, but they ignore that
agency has no obligation to act on their preferred timeframe. Compelling the agency
to act now causes irreparable harm, both by “improperly intrud[ing] on a coordinate 
branch,” Trump v. California, No. 26A139, slip op. 9 (Aug. 24, 2026), and by rushing 
the agency into issuing a decision before it has had the opportunity to receive, much 
less consider, public comments on the broadcasters’ overlapping application. 
The challengers similarly err in contending (Opp. 23-24) that, because the 
Fourth Circuit merely ordered the FCC to act and did not issue a final decision on the 
merits, the party committees do not face irreparable harm. In their petition for a writ 
of mandamus below, the challengers emphasized that the Fourth Circuit panel had 
“already held” that the Media Bureau’s public notice “violates federal law.” C.A. Pet. 
for Mandamus 14. The panel, for its part, reiterated when issuing mandamus that it 
had already ruled that the public notice “is plainly contrary to law and cannot stand.” 
Appl. App. 9a. The whole point of the mandamus order is thus to “allow the [panel] 
to reach the merits and recapitulate its own earlier conclusions, disrupting settled

9 
campaign finance rules in the hot breath of an impending election.” Id. at 28a (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). At a minimum, the Fourth Circuit’s order creates significant 
uncertainty about what rates broadcasters may charge for the rest of the election 
cycle. “Neither parties nor candidates nor broadcasters have any idea how to plan, 
contractually or otherwise, for the rest of the election season.” Id. at 25a. That uncertainty amounts to irreparable harm. 
The challengers identify no equities that outweigh those serious harms. They 
contend (Opp. 23) that “broadcasters are being compelled to offer substantial unlawful discounts to party committees and [joint fundraising committees],” but they have 
no standing to invoke the broadcasters’ interests. Indeed, it is telling that the broadcasters, the entities most directly affected by the Media Bureau’s public notice, have 
not sought immediate judicial intervention and are content to allow FCC proceedings 
to continue. The challengers separately complain (Opp. 27) that the Media Bureau’s 
public notice enables “parties and [joint fundraising committees] to blanket the airwaves with discount advertising”—i.e., to engage in more political speech for less 
money. But the challengers’ desire to mute their opponents’ political speech is not a 
cognizable harm, much less an adequate basis for denying a stay of the Fourth Circuit’s indefensible mandamus order. 
* * * * * 
This Court should stay the court of appeals’ order pending the filing and disposition of a petition for a writ of certiorari. 
Respectfully submitted.
D. JOHN SAUER
 Solicitor General 
OCTOBER 2026
